## 1. GLOBAL MACRO OVERVIEW

The macro backdrop on 28 May 2026 is defined by the collision of sticky inflation and decelerating growth — a classically uncomfortable environment for central banks and risk assets alike. The US PCE price index accelerated in April at its fastest annual rate in three years, driven primarily by surging energy costs linked to the ongoing US-Iran military conflict, which has shuttered the Strait of Hormuz and disrupted global oil supply chains. Core PCE rose 3.3% year-on-year in April, up from 3.2% in March, solidifying expectations that the Fed will keep rates on hold well into next year, with a growing minority now pricing a hike before year-end. [Source: https://www.reuters.com/business/us-pce-inflation-firmer-april-2026-05-28/]

The growth backdrop has deteriorated further after the Commerce Department revised Q1 2026 GDP growth down to a 1.6% annualised pace, from an initial 2.0% estimate, adding to concerns that the US economy is losing momentum precisely as inflation reaccelerates. [Source: https://www.wsj.com/economy/gdp-growth-revised-lower-for-first-quarter-e1a6ff93] Against this backdrop, Fed Governor Lisa Cook stated on 27 May that she is "prepared to raise rates if needed," echoing a hawkish shift across the committee. CME FedWatch now prices a 40% probability of a rate hike at the December meeting, up from just 3% at the June meeting level. [Source: https://www.cbsnews.com/news/kevin-warsh-federal-reserve-inflation-challenges/]

Equity markets are showing remarkable resilience, with Goldman Sachs raising its S&P 500 year-end target to 8,000 from 7,600, citing earnings growth as the primary driver. The S&P 500 currently trades at 7,537.90, up 9% year-to-date, with AI-driven semiconductor demand providing a powerful earnings tailwind — South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix joined Micron in the $1 trillion market cap club. [Source: https://www.businessinsider.com/stock-market-outlook-sp500-8000-earnings-eps-goldman-sachs-forecast-2026-5] The VIX has settled at 16.15, suggesting equity markets remain relatively sanguine despite the macro crosscurrents. [Source: Yahoo Finance (^VIX)]

Treasury markets reflect the stagflationary tension: the 10-year yield sits at 4.50% and the 2-year at 4.01%, generating a positive but still relatively flat yield curve. [Source: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DGS10] The effective Fed Funds Rate stands at 3.64%, still well below CPI of 3.95%, meaning real rates remain modestly negative — a configuration that historically supports hard assets. The DXY Dollar Index has slipped to 99.02, its recovery from the Iran war lows showing signs of stalling near the critical 100.60 neckline level identified by technical analysts. [Source: Yahoo Finance (DX-Y.NYB)]

Global growth concerns are broadening. The African Development Bank cut Africa's 2026 growth forecast to 4.2% from 4.4%, citing Middle East energy cost pass-through. The ECB has issued a formal warning that financial markets are underestimating geopolitical and fiscal risks, with its Financial Stability Review cautioning that market moves in response to the Middle East conflict have been "orderly" but reflect complacency. [Source: https://www.wsj.com/pro/central-banking/financial-markets-underestimate-geopolitical-and-fiscal-risks-ecb-warns-55e8f322]

### Disputed

- [Gold is trading higher today, described as "rebounding from a two-month low"]: Partially conflicting data. The data bundle (Yahoo Finance GC=F) shows gold at $4,491.10 (+0.98%), consistent with a rebound. However, CNBC's 28 May article titled "Gold hits two-month low" (published 04:56 GMT today) reported gold futures falling 1.6% to $4,377.10 on that same date. The report's current-session gain of +0.98% to $4,491 represents a meaningful intraday reversal from levels reported earlier this morning — the report does not adequately flag this intraday complexity and presents the picture as straightforwardly bullish when the earlier session was sharply down.

- [Report states "Brent futures falling toward $93 a barrel" referencing WSJ source]: The WSJ livecoverage (dated 27 May) states Brent falling toward $93, but today's Yahoo Finance data shows Brent at $92.04 (−2.39%), already below $93. The directional claim is broadly correct but the specific price reference from that source is stale (yesterday's data). The Brent data from OilPrice.com news snippets (published around the same time, 26–28 May) show wildly inconsistent Brent prices ranging from ~$92 to $100.10 depending on the article, indicating significant intraday volatility not fully captured in the report's single-price presentation.

- [Report characterises real rates as "modestly negative" — Fed Funds at 3.64% vs CPI at 3.95%]: Technically accurate on the nominal spread, but this comparison uses the Fed Funds effective rate (3.64%, data as of April 1) against CPI (3.95%, also as of April 1). The 10-year real yield, which is more relevant for hard asset analysis, is not directly available in the bundle. The characterisation is directionally reasonable but methodologically imprecise for a trading report; the real rate on the 10-year (4.50% nominal vs ~3.95% CPI) would actually be modestly *positive*, contradicting the "historically supports hard assets" framing.

- [Report states the US PCE print was "released today" and is the "single most important variable for today's session"]: The Reuters article (published 12:40 GMT 28 May) confirms PCE was released today. However, the CBS News article (26 May) had pre-release consensus at 3.9% annual PCE headline, while the Reuters article cites the actual print without giving the precise headline PCE YoY figure — only core PCE at 3.3% is explicitly confirmed in the bundle. The report does not cite the headline PCE figure, only core, yet repeatedly references the print as confirming the "fastest pace in three years," which is stated in the Reuters article but without a specific headline number being verifiable in the bundle.
